title: Buying a used BMW E90: What you can find out in 30 minutes
seoTitle: Buying a used BMW E90: What you can find out in 30 minutes
description: A three-part viewing worksheet for checking paperwork, inspecting the car, and deciding what to investigate next.
body:
The wheels are the first thing you notice at a viewing. Whether the last repair is documented often takes longer to figure out. Split the first half-hour into three parts: paperwork, the car, and unanswered questions. Allow separate time for the test drive and any professional inspection.

**Minutes 0–10: Check the paperwork.** Ask for service invoices and inspection reports. Record the date and mileage for important work. “It was done” is a statement. “Invoice from March at 132,000 km” gives you something you can check.

**Minutes 10–20: Walk around the car.** Describe what you can see without diagnosing it. Write “different paint shade on the right-hand door,” rather than “accident damage.” If you’re unsure, get an independent inspection. The 318i badge alone doesn’t tell you which engine, equipment, or parts the car has.

**Minutes 20–30: Decide what’s missing.** Take unanswered questions home. You don’t have to buy the car at the viewing.

| Viewing worksheet | Notes |
|---|---|
| Variant, year, mileage | |
| Last documented service | |
| What I noticed and what the seller said | |
| Question for a professional inspection | |
| Next step: investigate, request a quote, or walk away | |

For a more detailed inspection checklist, see [ADAC](https://www.adac.de/rund-ums-fahrzeug/auto-kaufen-verkaufen/gebrauchtwagenkauf/gebrauchtwagen-kaufen/) or [TÜV NORD](https://www.tuev-nord.de/de/wissen/ratgeber-und-tipps-mobilitaet/tipps-zum-gebrauchtwagenkauf/). The [BMW 318i E90 diary](/en/journal/bmw-318i-e90-kosten) shows how to start a record after the purchase.

title: What does your car cost per month? Start with the receipts
seoTitle: What does your car cost per month? Start with the receipts
description: Work out your monthly car costs from twelve months of receipts, with a table and a worked example.
body:
The fuel receipt is easy to find. The annual insurance bill and the set of tyres are easier to forget. Start with everything you actually paid over the last twelve months. Then turn it into a monthly average.

| Category | What to include | Total |
|---|---|---:|
| Fixed costs | Insurance, vehicle tax, parking space | €___ |
| Driving | Fuel or charging | €___ |
| Upkeep | Workshop bills, servicing, tyres, inspection fees | €___ |
| Projects | Mods, accessories, tools bought for a project | €___ |
| Monthly average | Recorded payments divided by 12 | €___ |

Enter an annual bill once. If you divide it into monthly amounts for comparison, don’t count those amounts as additional spending. Leave missing figures blank.

**Worked example, not a BMW cost estimate:** €600 fixed costs, €1,200 fuel, €480 upkeep, and €120 projects add up to €2,400 a year, or €200 a month. Financing and depreciation aren’t included. If you want to compare the total cost of owning two cars, consider depreciation too. Keep the cash you paid separate so you can still answer “What actually left my account?”

[ADAC’s car cost overview](https://www.adac.de/rund-ums-fahrzeug/auto-kaufen-verkaufen/autokosten/uebersicht/) distinguishes fixed costs, running costs, workshop spending, and depreciation. The [E90 diary](/en/journal/bmw-318i-e90-kosten) shows how to keep unpublished figures out of the total.

title: The first 30 days with a used car: What I’d check first
seoTitle: The first 30 days with a used car: What I’d check first
description: A simple plan for the first day, week, and month, with a worksheet for sorting the paperwork and open questions.
body:
Once you buy a car, the wish list usually starts filling up. I’d make a shorter list first: **documented, open, later**. It makes it easier to see which question needs an answer today.

**Day one:** Write down the mileage at handover and collect the available paperwork. Separate what the seller or workshop told you from what you can verify yourself.

**Week one:** Sort the unanswered questions. If there’s a warning message or a suspected safety issue, get it checked before continuing to use the car. For scheduled maintenance, consult the relevant owner’s manual and service history. Gaps in the paperwork don’t establish a service schedule.

**By the end of the month:** Pick the next open item. Get a quote and set aside time if needed. Then decide how much you want to spend on the first mod.

| Status | Example | Next step |
|---|---|---|
| Documented | Oil service with date and mileage | File the record |
| Open | No evidence of the last filter change | Check paperwork and establish what’s due |
| Later | Different wheels are on the wish list | Note the idea; hold off ordering |

This worksheet helps organise what you know. It doesn’t replace a vehicle inspection. For the buying stage, start with the [ADAC checklist](https://www.adac.de/rund-ums-fahrzeug/auto-kaufen-verkaufen/gebrauchtwagenkauf/gebrauchtwagen-kaufen/). Keep documented jobs together in [CapCar Garage](/garage).

title: The €200 part: What a car mod can really cost
seoTitle: The €200 part: What a car mod can really cost
description: Compare two upgrade quotes after shipping, paint, fitting, and accessories are included.
body:
The shopping cart shows you the price of the part. Your actual budget might still need shipping, mounting hardware, paint, and labour. Find out what’s included before you order. If paperwork or an inspection needs to be sorted out, leave the decision open until you’ve checked it.

Start by describing what you want finished on the car. Ask both suppliers to price the same scope. If one quote includes paint and the other doesn’t, comparing just the part prices won’t tell you much.

| Item | Example A | Example B |
|---|---:|---:|
| Part | €200 | €250 |
| Shipping | €25 | €15 |
| Preparation and paint | €110 | Included |
| Fitting and accessories | €85 | €85 |
| **Planned total** | **€420** | **€350** |

These are illustrative figures. They exclude any additional inspection costs and contingency. Put your contingency in the budget, but keep it out of actual spending. Once the work is done, record what you paid next to the original estimate. That difference will help you price the next job.

Before buying, write down what’s included, what’s confirmed for your exact vehicle, and the total at which you’d rather wait.

Add your own numbers in the [upgrade calculator in the E90 diary](/en/journal/bmw-318i-e90-kosten). Use the [Project Car Planner](/project-car-planner) when you’re ready to make a parts and tasks list.

title: A maintenance record you’ll still understand in two years
seoTitle: A maintenance record you’ll still understand in two years
description: A copyable service record for the date, mileage, work, parts, receipts, and anything still open.
body:
“Filter done” makes sense today. Two years from now, which filter was it? What was the mileage? Where’s the receipt? A useful maintenance entry answers those questions without taking up a page.

Copy this into your notes or service log:

```text
Date and mileage:
Reason or observation:
Work completed:
Who did the work?
Part, manufacturer, or part number:
Amount paid and receipt reference:
Anything still open?
```

For a cabin filter, the work field could read: “Cabin filter replaced; photographed the old part and the new packaging.” Record only what you actually paid. Leave the amount blank if you haven’t found the receipt. Say whether you did the work yourself or had a workshop do it.

If the work is still pending, write “planned” or “part ordered.” That way it can’t be mistaken for completed maintenance. If you share a summary when selling the car, leave out personal information the recipient doesn’t need.

Use the template on paper or attach the work to your vehicle in [CapCar Garage](/garage). The [E90 diary](/en/journal/bmw-318i-e90-kosten) also includes a printable checklist.

title: Comparing two workshop quotes: Five questions to ask
seoTitle: Comparing two workshop quotes: Five questions to ask
description: Compare what each quote includes and copy a short message asking for an itemised price.
body:
“Service: €350” sounds clear enough. If another quote says “€420 including filters and brake fluid,” you still don’t know whether both workshops are quoting for the same job. Ask for a short breakdown before comparing prices. You can refer back to it when the work is finished.

| Question | Workshop A | Workshop B |
|---|---|---|
| What work is included? | | |
| Which parts and fluids are included? | | |
| Are diagnosis, materials, and disposal included? | | |
| What is the total including VAT? | | |
| How will we agree on additional work? | | |

**Message to copy:**

> Hi, I’m comparing quotes for the same job. Could you tell me what work and parts are included, the total including VAT, and when you’d call me before doing any additional work? I can send the vehicle details and mileage.

After the appointment, record what was agreed, what was done, and what appears on the invoice. If there’s a difference, ask about the specific line item.

Some faults need diagnosis before a workshop can price a repair. Ask what that first step involves rather than expecting a firm repair quote upfront. Use [CapCar Garage](/garage) to keep the quote, completed work, and outstanding items separate.

title: Buying car parts online: A quick fitment checklist
seoTitle: Buying car parts online: A quick fitment checklist
description: Check vehicle variant, part numbers, the source of the fitment claim, and what comes in the box.
body:
The part in the photo looks like the old one. The listing says “fits BMW 3 Series.” Both are starting points, but neither confirms it fits your car. Gather the vehicle details and any available part references before comparing listings.

| Check | What to record |
|---|---|
| Vehicle | Year, body style, engine, and relevant equipment |
| Starting point | The existing part number or other documentation, if available |
| Listing | Manufacturer, part number, and any restrictions |
| Confirmation | The reliable source that confirms fitment |
| What’s included | Anything you’ll need to get separately |
| Decision | Confirmed, question outstanding, or ruled out |

**Example:** Two listings name the same model but show different part numbers. Instead of picking the cheaper one, ask whether it fits your exact variant and save the reply alongside the listing. For safety-critical parts or unclear compatibility, ask a qualified professional to check.

Record where you got the number. A number from an advert isn’t the same as one read from the original part. If a question is still open, leave the item on your wish list until you have an answer.

Use the [CapCar Project Car Planner](/project-car-planner) to keep the listing and your unanswered question together.

title: Three car photos in one place: A shot list to save
seoTitle: Three car photos in one place: A shot list to save
description: A simple phone photography shot list: the setting, the shape of the car, and one detail.
body:
A good photo stop doesn’t have to be dramatic. Start with somewhere you can park without blocking anyone. Then look for the trees, wall, or view you want in the frame. If a shot only works from an active lane, find a different angle or move on.

| Shot | What it shows | Phone tip |
|---|---|---|
| Wide | The car in its setting | Leave room around the car and choose the background deliberately |
| Three-quarter | The shape and proportions | Step back and try a different height |
| Detail | Something specific to your car | Try a wheel, tail light, or part of the interior |

Try to get all three with the car parked in one place. If the background looks busy, move the camera a few steps sideways. Shoot the same angle from a different height and choose the better one later.

For next time, note where you parked, when the light worked, and which way you faced. That’s what makes a photo useful to someone who wants to try the spot themselves. Before sharing, consider whether recognisable people, number plates, or private details need to appear.

Browse the [CapCar Roadbook](/roadbook) for more ideas and take the shot list with you.

title: A short Rheingau drive from Rüsselsheim: Eltville and Niederwald
seoTitle: A short Rheingau drive from Rüsselsheim: Eltville and Niederwald
description: A researched two-stop drive idea with a planning worksheet for parking, walking, and the return.
body:
I’d rather have two worthwhile stops than five I’m already thinking about leaving. This short trip pairs **Eltville’s Rhine waterfront** with the **Niederwald Monument**: time by the water, a view, and a return without rushing.

**Stop one: Eltville.** Park in a designated space and walk to the river. The [town of Eltville describes the promenade as car-free](https://www.eltville.de/freizeit-tourismus/erleben-entdecken/sehenswuerdigkeiten/eltville/rheinufer/). If you want a photo of the car, find a different place where you can park. This is a good stop for coffee, whether you buy it or bring it.

**Stop two: Niederwald Monument.** Check the [official visitor information](https://www.schloesser-hessen.de/de/osteinscher-niederwald/besucherinformation) for access and parking. Include the walk from the car park, especially if you want to arrive in time for a particular light.

| Before you leave | Your plan |
|---|---|
| Start and latest return | |
| Car park and walk for each stop | |
| Which stop stays if you’re short on time? | |
| Alternative for rain or fading daylight | |

This is a researched route idea, not a first-hand account. Check the actual drive time from your starting point and decide which stop is optional. For a longer version that includes Biebrich, read the [Rüsselsheim to Rheingau day-trip guide](/en/journal/ruesselsheim-rheingau-tagesausflug), or browse the [Roadbook](/roadbook).

title: Plan a road trip with AI: A prompt that works with your four-hour limit
seoTitle: Plan a road trip with AI: A prompt that works with your four-hour limit
description: Copy a four-hour loop prompt and check the suggested stops, parking, and return time before driving.
body:
“Plan a scenic drive” leaves a lot unsaid. If you need to be back at six, that matters as much as the view. Give the planner a starting point, tell it what you want to see, and make clear that breaks count towards the time available.

Copy this prompt and change the place names:

> I’m starting in Rüsselsheim and need to be back there four hours later. Plan a relaxed loop through the Rheingau with a stretch overlooking the Rhine, a coffee stop, and a short photo stop. Include parking, walking, and breaks within the four hours. Give me an address or a clearly identifiable location for each stop, plus a shorter option in case I leave late. Flag any opening hours, access details, or drive times I still need to verify.

**Check the result in this order:**

1. Do the start and finish match, and can you follow the loop in your navigation app?
2. Does each stop have somewhere to park and a realistic walk from the car?
3. Do the breaks fit the time limit? Which stop could you drop?
4. Do the important details agree with official visitor information?

Afterwards, make three notes: **What did I keep? What did I skip? What would I plan earlier next time?** That turns a one-off answer into a route you can reuse or recommend. Try the prompt in the [CapCar AI Trip Planner](/ai) or your preferred assistant.
